question: Seven claims seen on adverts and labels. Which promise something you could check, and which promise almost nothing?
answer: The empty ones are built from words that bend: up to, helps, proven, recommend. Each stays true across a huge range of meanings, so advertisers can use them safely. A checkable claim names a number and a baseline, so it could turn out wrong, and the seller can be held to it.
move: Trust a claim in proportion to how easily it could be shown wrong.
ask: Which thing did I buy because of a word that promised nothing?

items.note: On a banner across a shop window.
items.verdict: Up to sets a ceiling. Most items can be cut by far less, or not at all.
Helps covers any effect at all, however small.
A unit price lets you compare any two packs, whatever their size.
Colgate's survey let dentists name several brands. Britain's ad watchdog banned it.

items.note: On a jar of face cream.
items.verdict: Proven to do what, in how many people, against what? The phrase never says.
A firm promise with a date on it. If the price rises, you can hold them to it.
A number and a baseline. Check the baseline, but you can check it.

reference: Advertising Standards Authority, ASA adjudication on Colgate-Palmolive (UK) Ltd, 2007; Weasel word, Oxford English Dictionary
